transcript.text: Hi Ritika, thanks for joining. I'm on the hiring team for this role, and I'd like to understand your experience in some depth. We have about 10 minutes, with time for your questions at the end. What is one useful idea from your PGDHRM studies that you have applied recently?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: um okay so firstly thank you for the question actually I think that’s a really interesting one and I do have something in mind so one idea from my PGDHRM that I’ve quite recently applied practically was around the concept of psychological safety in teams so in our organisational behaviour module at IIM Ranchi we really went into this idea that unless people feel safe to speak up especially junior employees or newcomers then a lot of problems just stay under the surface and don’t come out and funny enough I got to see this in action during my summer internship at Mahindra and Mahindra in Nashik so what happened was that I was designing this onboarding buddy program for diploma trainees and initially I was just thinking of it as you know like a checklist help them relocate and settle but then I remembered from class this discussion we had about climate of openness and how a buddy system can foster it not just on paper but really by encouraging new hires to share concerns or confusion without fearing embarrassment so I tweaked the plan a bit and rather than just pairing people up randomly I tried to match them with buddies who had come through similar backgrounds like diploma colleges from small towns um and I also encouraged the buddies to share their own funny mistakes from their first year so as to normalise asking questions and actually for the feedback part after five days we had these reflection circles and some trainees said they found it easier to ask things they felt silly about otherwise so I guess that whole thing about psychological safety wasn’t just theoretical but something that really influenced how I built the program and it was interesting because many of the IR team members who helped me run it also shared that shopfloor employees often hesitate to come to HR directly which was exactly what we learned in OB so in short that’s one idea I consciously took from the classroom to the plant and um it actually had a real-life impact at least based on what I saw and the feedback we got from that first cohort
Thank you. Walk me through your background: your studies and the experiences that led you to HR.
transcript.why: Your example showed how you applied a classroom idea while designing the onboarding buddy program, so I moved on to your broader background.

transcript.text:
yeah so I’ll just walk you through my journey actually um like I think for me it all started with my undergrad in psychology at LSR in Delhi which is sort of where I first got exposed to human behaviour in depth so originally honestly when I joined psychology I didn’t have HR specifically in mind it was more like I was curious about why people do what they do you know like those small things in teams how group dynamics change how some leaders are able to motivate and others aren’t and so on so that curiosity led me to get involved in the Psychology Society over the three years and by the final year I was quite active I even became president and we ran events involving workplace wellbeing, mental health at work and talks with some alumni in HR who sort of planted the idea in my head that hey maybe this could actually be a career option, not just academia or counselling

then what really made things click was when I did this internship as a recruitment intern at Teach For India during my final year so my main role was screening applications and doing initial phone interviews and that was honestly my first hands-on taste of, you can say, selection processes and how tough it is to judge people not just on marks or resumes but on softer things like intent, motivation, grit and how that can make or break culture so I realised um I quite enjoyed talking to people, figuring out the fit, and also the larger mission aspect that draws certain kinds of people in

after graduating I was sure I wanted to explore HR deeper and that’s what led me to prepare for and join IIM Ranchi for the PGDHRM because it’s one of the top schools for HR you know and here I got even broader exposure like through classroom learning which is quite rigorous but also committee work—in my case with the placement committee where I interact with recruiters regularly—plus the summer internship with Mahindra where it was the first time I saw HR on the factory floor and IR issues which are totally different from more corporate-type settings so through all this the thread has really been my fascination with how people are selected, developed and sometimes even pushed out of organisations and how HR sits at that crossroad not just as rule enforcer but as a kind of builder of culture so um yeah I’d say it wasn’t a super straight line but all these pieces together brought me here and I feel like HR is this nice intersection of psychology, business and real life people problems that just keeps me interested
I see you analysed exit interviews at Mahindra & Mahindra. What did you personally do first with that information?
transcript.why: Your answer traced how psychology, recruitment exposure, HR studies, and the Mahindra internship led you toward HR. I’m moving to the specific analysis work you described on your resume.

transcript.text:
oh yeah that project was honestly a real learning curve for me so when I got the exit interview data it was all in quite a raw form like there were these handwritten notes and Excel sheets collected by different HR executives so first step honestly was just to clean all this data and make it usable which is always way more messy than people imagine and I remember spending a good week just trying to reconcile names and employee IDs and like fill in gaps where someone had only written “better prospect” or “personal reasons” so I basically tried to go a bit deeper wherever I could asking the local HR folks who had conducted the interviews if they remembered specifics and once that was done I started categorising the reasons into buckets which had come out in our HR analytics class so like, you know, pay, work environment, shift allocation and so on

but the really interesting part came when—I still remember this—I was manually going through some of the comments and a pattern started emerging about shift allocation like people saying they weren’t ready for night shifts in the first six months or had family issues no one listened to and you know initially I thought this is just the usual shopfloor thing but then when I looked specifically at first-year exits there was a big spike for shift-related reasons which, like, honestly surprised a couple of people on the IR team too because people just assume wages or permanent jobs are the main reason but that wasn’t the case for these associates

so with that observation I made a small presentation first for my project mentor just to say here’s what I’m finding and here’s why I think it matters and then I started digging a little deeper like okay is this issue specific to one line or shift or is it something broad and that led me to do sort of a basic cross-tab in Excel by line and by timing of exit and, um, later on when it seemed to be concentrated on two lines which were piloting a rotation-based system I kind of flagged it to my mentor and we spoke to the plant HR head together

so basically the first thing was to make sense of the messy data and then share some early patterns that seemed actionable and that actually led to the idea for a shift-preference trial window but before all that I guess the immediate thing was context-building and just, um, being curious enough to ask if a so-called generic reason could have deeper patterns behind it you know
When you discussed the shift-preference trial with your mentor and the plant HR head, which decisions in shaping the proposal were yours?
transcript.why: Your answer explained how you cleaned and analysed the data, but it was less clear which decisions in the proposal were specifically yours. I asked about your individual contribution before checking the 58% figure.

transcript.text:
okay so that meeting with my mentor and the plant HR head was honestly quite a learning experience because like I’d done some small projects before but this was the first time I was actually part of recommending a change that would affect so many people in a live setting so what happened was after we’d noticed that pattern about shift allocation I sat down with my mentor first just to brainstorm how we could even test if giving associates some choice would make a difference but there were a lot of practical constraints coming up you know because shopfloor scheduling is tightly linked to production volumes, and there was a bit of resistance even from IR because they were like if we open the floodgates and let everyone pick, it’ll disrupt the whole rota so I was the one who did the initial proposal to do this in a really limited pilot, like not across the entire plant, and to propose a time-bound window when new diploma trainees, basically in their joining month, could submit their preference for shift—not a guarantee, but at least a structured way to register it, you know, that was something I insisted we frame really clearly so it’s not a promise but more an “option to express” kind of thing

also um another aspect which I pushed for was using a simple preference form, actually just on paper, not digital because some associates were not comfortable with apps and all so that actually made it less threatening for them and IR teams could collect it easily so that was a small on-ground tweak I suggested based on what I’d observed during orientation meetings

when we were finalising how to monitor the pilot, I insisted that we track the take-up line-wise and share feedback both ways like from associates and line supervisors because sometimes you know management tries something and people on the floor don’t even know why or what it is, so I was like can we do simple feedback check-ins after one month to see if people even felt it had made any difference or if they thought it was all just paperwork which sometimes happens in factories

so yeah I mean, while my mentor and the HR head had the final say about which lines to involve and the exact timing, I think the shape of the pilot—a preference window, a non-digital form, the feedback mechanism—those were areas where I actively contributed and tried to keep the design grounded in what I was hearing from associates, not just what looked nice on paper, and it kind of brought together both what I’d learnt in class and what seemed realistic in the factory context
You described the pilot design clearly. What was the comparison behind the 58% figure in your analysis?
transcript.why: You explained which parts of the pilot design were yours. I asked about the 58% figure to understand how that result was calculated.

transcript.text:
oh right yeah so that 58 percent figure I mentioned—actually that was one of the numbers that really stood out for me when I was doing the analysis, so what I basically did was, I took all the exit interviews for shop-floor associates leaving within their first year of joining, right, and out of this sample I had, I think it was 380 cases in total, so first thing was to just get the entire bunch of reasons cited, although like I said earlier, a lot of them were scribbled notes you know like “personal issues,” or “family,” or “not comfortable with shift” but I decided to specifically focus on what was coming up again and again in their own words so I made these main buckets like pay, career growth, supervisor conflict, and then shift allocation or timing, so once I had that, I just did a basic count to see which reason showed up at least once in the exit notes for each person, even if sometimes people listed more than one reason, I just took the dominant one—usually the first thing mentioned

so the 58 percent, what it means is: out of all the first-year shopfloor exits, that proportion had cited shift allocation or inadequate notice for shift changes as either the main or second-most important reason for leaving, so it wasn’t like just a few people complaining, it was actually by far the biggest single reason above pay or supervisor complaints, at least in this segment—now, important to mention, I did try to compare this percentage across tenure groups, so like those who left after two years or more, and in that set, shift allocation was much lower as a cited reason, I think below 20 percent, so clearly something was happening with the very new joiners, particularly diploma trainees or lateral shop-floor hires who had limited say in their initial allocation

and I know there’s always a risk of over-relying on self-reported exit interviews but this alignment between what people said while leaving and also what HR folks on the ground informally told me made it quite significant for recommending that pilot, so to sum up, the 58 percent is a share of early leavers for whom shift issues were a strong enough factor to be written down or remembered, and that comparison of early versus longer-tenured exits really made the number jump out for us during the discussion with my mentor and the plant HR head
Let’s move to your recruitment work at Teach For India. What did you have to judge during the first-round phone interviews?
transcript.why: This question checked how the 58% figure was calculated and what it was compared with, building on your description of the exit analysis.

transcript.text:
oh yeah so with Teach For India that was actually my first experience doing something even remotely close to selection interviewing and I have to say I really got a lot of perspective from it because you know before that I always thought interviews were mostly about checking skills or academic background, but TFI’s first round was way more focused on what they call intent and alignment so before we even began interviews the training we got from the senior recruitment managers was about looking for very specific things beyond just how well someone speaks or their resume points so in each call we were supposed to judge not just basic eligibility like graduation status or English proficiency—which was sometimes an issue—but also deeper motivations

so for example a huge part of the process was trying to get a sense of why someone actually wanted to join TFI as a fellow because the fellowship is two years of teaching in under-resourced schools with a lot of challenges and the drop-out rate can get pretty significant, so there’s this focus on finding people who have a clear personal reason or, like, a story that connects them to the mission rather than just someone looking for a gap year or a backup to a corporate job so we would ask about what drew them to apply, about any volunteering experience, but more important was how they reflected on those experiences, like did they talk about impact, about learning, about working with kids and all that

another thing we were specifically told to probe was resilience and adaptability because honestly, a lot of fellows go in with good intentions but it’s a tough job—you’re dealing with classroom management, sometimes lack of support, really long hours and so on—and so even in that short phone call we’d ask about a tough situation they’d faced, any time they felt out of place or failed, and see not just what happened but how they described recovering from it or what they learnt so it was less about the perfect answer and more about self-awareness and, I think, a bit of humility, like were they able to recognize growth areas or did they just brush over challenges

one more factor we were told to keep in mind was their understanding of what TFI actually does because sometimes we saw applicants who would mix it up with other NGOs or think it was only about CSR or glamorous impact, but we needed to gauge if they really understood the ground reality and were signing up for the right reasons so part of my job was to ask questions to clarify those misconceptions and see their reactions

so overall I’d say what I was really judging in those first round interviews was a blend of intent, a kind of value alignment, some evidence of having dealt with ambiguity or hardship, and clarity about what the role actually meant, and of course the basics like communication and professionalism on the call but the softer elements were often the deciding factors for shortlisting whether an applicant should move forward or not
Which decisions in those first-round calls were yours personally when you recommended someone for the next stage?
transcript.why: Your answer described what interviewers were expected to look for, but not your own part in conducting the calls and reaching a recommendation. I asked about how you personally handled that process.

transcript.text:
so actually in those first-round calls with Teach For India, the whole process was designed to be quite structured but there was still a fairly significant element of personal judgment that came in, like you’re given a rubric of what to look for and a template for scoring but after a point it really does come down to your individual read of the person—so for every call I did, after completing the set list of questions I had to fill out this interviewer evaluation sheet, right, where I’d rate things like intent, alignment with TFI’s mission, adaptability, and communication, and along with the scores there was a comment box where I had to explain my rationale, in my own words, as to why I thought someone should or shouldn’t move to the next stage

so decisions that were really mine personally, I’d say, first and foremost, were how I chose to interpret their answers and place weight on certain responses versus others—like, there were some applicants who had decent academic or work backgrounds, but the way they spoke about volunteering was very superficial, like “I wanted to try it for experience,” and when I probed, it didn’t go very deep, so even if they ticked some eligibility boxes, I sometimes decided not to recommend them because I felt that lack of mission fit would become an issue later on and you could sense their motivation wasn’t strong enough for the toughness of the fellowship

on the flip side there were cases where someone’s English might be slightly shaky or they’d be clearly nervous but they had really raw, honest reasons for applying and would give quite heartfelt stories, like tutoring siblings through school, or being deeply motivated by personal struggle in their own education, and with those, even if the “polish” wasn’t there, I would often recommend them onwards, writing in the comments that their intent and resilience outweighed a few communication gaps because TFI has support systems for training anyway

I also decided what kind of follow-up questions to ask in the moment—sometimes if someone gave a really short answer about a challenge, I’d dig deeper, and how I interpreted what came up there also shaped my recommendation—you know, if someone got defensive or dismissive about failures, I was less likely to push for them, but if they reflected thoughtfully, that would really weigh in their favour

of course, my recommendations weren’t the final decision—someone from the senior team would review the call notes and sometimes listen to call recordings if there was a borderline case—but I’d say my summaries and logic in the evaluation were taken pretty seriously for most of the calls, so the decision of whether to advocate for a candidate or not, and how strongly I did so in the written comments, that was fully based on my own judgment during and after the call
Across the 40 first-round interviews, how many did you recommend for the next stage?
transcript.why: You explained which judgments were yours and how you recorded them, so I asked about the outcome across the 40 interviews.

transcript.text:
oh okay so actually across those 40 first-round interviews I did at Teach For India, if I remember right, I recommended around—let me think, yeah—about 13 or 14 candidates for the next stage, so roughly a third or just under that moved forward based on my evaluation um but you know this wasn’t actually fixed, like there was no quota or anything it just depended on the strength of the applicant pool week to week, and there were some days where literally none of the three or four people I spoke to in a row made it to the next round which honestly felt a bit awkward at first because you kind of want to give everyone some hope, but the bar for mission alignment and resilience was set pretty high so sometimes it was just clear that it wouldn’t be a good fit no matter how much you wanted to be encouraging

and then there were a couple of calls where I was genuinely on the fence, like it could have gone either way depending on how you weigh their responses—as in they’d have a strong personal story but maybe not so much clarity on the actual demands of teaching full-time—so in those borderline cases I tried to err on the side of giving them a shot if they showed openness to learning, especially because I knew the next rounds would probe teaching aptitude more deeply

what was interesting is that sometimes we’d discuss “confusing” cases with senior recruitment fellows, like if an applicant had a great volunteering background but seemed only half committed, or if their reasons for applying were very vague but you sensed some potential, and sometimes the consensus was to move them forward just to see how they handled the more intensive selection steps but yeah overall, if you look at my shortlist rate, I’d say it matched what TFI aimed for, which was not too high but not ultra-filtered either, because that first round was really about filtering out the clearly misaligned rather than choosing the polished finished product, if that makes sense and yeah, I guess by the end of my stint when I saw which of my recommended candidates actually went on to get offers or do well in later rounds, it was pretty satisfyi—well, not always predictable, but it made the process feel quite real and personal for me
Let’s switch to employee relations. A plant’s grievances rise sharply over one quarter. How would you determine whether the pattern points to a policy issue or a local management issue?
transcript.why: Your answer gave an approximate number of candidates you recommended and described how you handled borderline cases. The next question shifts to how you would diagnose a rise in employee grievances.

transcript.text:
oh that’s a great scenario actually because it’s something that came up during my time at Mahindra, not in quite as dramatic a spike, but tracking grievances across lines was a core part of what I worked on so here’s how I’d approach it, and sorry in advance, I always take a bit of a detour when I explain these things, but I find context helps—so let’s say you see grievances go up sharply in one quarter, first off I’d want to map out the data from your tracker by type, location, and time, just basic descriptive stuff so I’d rebuild a dashboard if there isn’t one already—which is kind of what happened in Nashik, where we moved our tracker from just a register to a line-wise, category-wise structure in Excel so you could filter by date raised, resolved, and so on

now, the main diagnostic I’d do is segmentation—is it a cluster in one department, one shopfloor line, or even one shift group, or is it spread more or less everywhere in the plant so if you see, for instance, that 40 out of 60 new grievances come from engine assembly line 3 and most are about, say, supervisor conduct, straight away you get a signal that it might be local management-related, possibly even down to one or two leaders or specific operational changes but if the surge is more in categories like attendance deductions, leave approvals or HR policies around, say, transfers, and it spans multiple lines, that leans toward a policy or systemic issue—sometimes a change in wage calculations, roster systems or a new attendance app triggers this and people across areas start raising a similar type of complaint

personally, what I found useful was also a quick pulse with team leads on the shopfloor or even talking informally to associates, because sometimes the tracker underreports grumbling till something blows up but one thing I’d pay a lot of attention to—and this is just from what I observed—is the language and escalation path of the grievances, like are people going directly to HR bypassing direct managers, are group grievances going up, or is it mostly individuals reporting isolated stuff? the more collective and formal it gets, the more it points to a policy or trust deficit with the system; if it’s the same names coming up as supervisors or managers, there’s more likely a local issue

of course, sometimes it’s both, especially if a poorly communicated policy change is left for line managers to handle and some struggle more than others but bottom line, my approach would be to start segmenting the data along all those axes—type, location, supervisor involved, timing around policy changes—then supplement that with a few targeted conversations, maybe even a quick dipstick survey if time permits, and only then would I start drawing up a root cause chart to present to the plant HR head or IR manager to see whether to review a plant-level policy or focus on coaching or re-training a specific set of managers

honestly, in the Nashik plant, we saw that cases would sometimes rise when there was just a new manager who wasn’t used to the team or vice versa so you can’t always jump to conclusions till you check the data against ground reality and stories you hear in the lunchroom or the union office but yeah, that’s how I’d try to separate out the signal between a systemic thing and something driven by local management conduct
Suppose the plant HR head needs an initial view within two days, while associates and supervisors give conflicting accounts. How would you prioritise the investigation?
transcript.why: You described several useful sources of evidence, so I asked how you would prioritise them when time is limited and accounts may conflict.

transcript.text:
oh wow yeah so the two-day deadline changes things quite a bit actually because normally you’d want to do a thorough deep dive but in this kind of time-crunched scenario the trick is to give a fact-based initial view without getting bogged down trying to solve every layer of the conflict, so my first move would basically be to lean really heavily on the objective data you have at hand, like whatever’s in the grievance tracker—dates, types, repeated names, escalation trends, those are things nobody can really dispute, so I’d quickly map out whether the spike is really a series of similar issues or a lot of noise from scattered causes and I’d pay immediate attention to any patterns you can see, even visually, whether certain supervisors’ names crop up in a majority of the new cases or if specific shifts or teams are recurrent

since you said associates and supervisors are giving quite different explanations, I’d probably do a structured rapid call or huddle with a representative group from both sides—maybe the senior-most associate rep on the affected line and the relevant supervisor, possibly even with line HR present as a neutral party, and in that chat I wouldn’t try to get to the full bottom of every individual story but would focus on establishing which issues recur most, not just anecdotes, so if several people mention the same policy confusion or the same team lead, that becomes part of my initial report whereas if it’s really just a clash of personalities in two or three isolated cases, I’d note that separately

to keep my initial view neutral, I’d also cross-reference with any written records—warning letters, shift roster changes, recent policy circulation emails—just to see if there was a trigger like a recent circular or event that might have caused this spike, because sometimes that’s exactly where the pattern lies and it saves you hours of speculation

one thing I learned from my Mahindra stint is that in a factory setup when you have to report up fast, narrative neutrality is really key—don’t try to judge intent or assign blame based on incomplete evidence, just tabulate what types of grievances are being raised, who’s involved, and whether there’s any temporal clustering around a recent process or personnel event and then in my summary to HR head, I’d say here’s the numbers by line, main categories of complaints, overlap in associate and supervisor accounts (if any), plus any immediate outlier findings like a new manager or recent leave rejection pattern and I would flag clearly where the accounts disagree—and where they match—so that management knows where to probe deeper after

and I wouldn’t try to “solve” the conflict fully in this first view—I’d just prioritise clarifying and reporting the scale, type, and most likely triggers based on what’s there, rather than trying to mediate or decide who’s right, which just isn’t feasible in two days—I guess that’s something I learned from watching the IR leads at Nashik, they were always very methodical about separating urgent reporting from the longer process of grievance closure, so I’d keep the first step as data-driven and as neutral as possible till we can dig in properly later
Thanks, Ritika. That’s everything from my side. What questions do you have for me?

yeah so I’ll just walk you through my journey actually um like I think for me it all started with my undergrad in psychology at LSR in Delhi which is sort of where I first got exposed to human behaviour in depth so originally honestly when I joined psychology I didn’t have HR specifically in mind it was more like I was curious about why people do what they do you know like those small things in teams how group dynamics change how some leaders are able to motivate and others aren’t and so on so that curiosity led me to get involved in the Psychology Society over the three years and by the final year I was quite active I even became president and we ran events involving workplace wellbeing, mental health at work and talks with some alumni in HR who sort of planted the idea in my head that hey maybe this could actually be a career option, not just academia or counselling

slot_transcript.candidate:
oh yeah that project was honestly a real learning curve for me so when I got the exit interview data it was all in quite a raw form like there were these handwritten notes and Excel sheets collected by different HR executives so first step honestly was just to clean all this data and make it usable which is always way more messy than people imagine and I remember spending a good week just trying to reconcile names and employee IDs and like fill in gaps where someone had only written “better prospect” or “personal reasons” so I basically tried to go a bit deeper wherever I could asking the local HR folks who had conducted the interviews if they remembered specifics and once that was done I started categorising the reasons into buckets which had come out in our HR analytics class so like, you know, pay, work environment, shift allocation and so on

but the really interesting part came when—I still remember this—I was manually going through some of the comments and a pattern started emerging about shift allocation like people saying they weren’t ready for night shifts in the first six months or had family issues no one listened to and you know initially I thought this is just the usual shopfloor thing but then when I looked specifically at first-year exits there was a big spike for shift-related reasons which, like, honestly surprised a couple of people on the IR team too because people just assume wages or permanent jobs are the main reason but that wasn’t the case for these associates

so with that observation I made a small presentation first for my project mentor just to say here’s what I’m finding and here’s why I think it matters and then I started digging a little deeper like okay is this issue specific to one line or shift or is it something broad and that led me to do sort of a basic cross-tab in Excel by line and by timing of exit and, um, later on when it seemed to be concentrated on two lines which were piloting a rotation-based system I kind of flagged it to my mentor and we spoke to the plant HR head together

so basically the first thing was to make sense of the messy data and then share some early patterns that seemed actionable and that actually led to the idea for a shift-preference trial window but before all that I guess the immediate thing was context-building and just, um, being curious enough to ask if a so-called generic reason could have deeper patterns behind it you know

slot_transcript.interviewer: When you discussed the shift-preference trial with your mentor and the plant HR head, which decisions in shaping the proposal were yours?
slot_transcript.candidate:
okay so that meeting with my mentor and the plant HR head was honestly quite a learning experience because like I’d done some small projects before but this was the first time I was actually part of recommending a change that would affect so many people in a live setting so what happened was after we’d noticed that pattern about shift allocation I sat down with my mentor first just to brainstorm how we could even test if giving associates some choice would make a difference but there were a lot of practical constraints coming up you know because shopfloor scheduling is tightly linked to production volumes, and there was a bit of resistance even from IR because they were like if we open the floodgates and let everyone pick, it’ll disrupt the whole rota so I was the one who did the initial proposal to do this in a really limited pilot, like not across the entire plant, and to propose a time-bound window when new diploma trainees, basically in their joining month, could submit their preference for shift—not a guarantee, but at least a structured way to register it, you know, that was something I insisted we frame really clearly so it’s not a promise but more an “option to express” kind of thing

turns.answer:
oh yeah so with Teach For India that was actually my first experience doing something even remotely close to selection interviewing and I have to say I really got a lot of perspective from it because you know before that I always thought interviews were mostly about checking skills or academic background, but TFI’s first round was way more focused on what they call intent and alignment so before we even began interviews the training we got from the senior recruitment managers was about looking for very specific things beyond just how well someone speaks or their resume points so in each call we were supposed to judge not just basic eligibility like graduation status or English proficiency—which was sometimes an issue—but also deeper motivations

so for example a huge part of the process was trying to get a sense of why someone actually wanted to join TFI as a fellow because the fellowship is two years of teaching in under-resourced schools with a lot of challenges and the drop-out rate can get pretty significant, so there’s this focus on finding people who have a clear personal reason or, like, a story that connects them to the mission rather than just someone looking for a gap year or a backup to a corporate job so we would ask about what drew them to apply, about any volunteering experience, but more important was how they reflected on those experiences, like did they talk about impact, about learning, about working with kids and all that

another thing we were specifically told to probe was resilience and adaptability because honestly, a lot of fellows go in with good intentions but it’s a tough job—you’re dealing with classroom management, sometimes lack of support, really long hours and so on—and so even in that short phone call we’d ask about a tough situation they’d faced, any time they felt out of place or failed, and see not just what happened but how they described recovering from it or what they learnt so it was less about the perfect answer and more about self-awareness and, I think, a bit of humility, like were they able to recognize growth areas or did they just brush over challenges

one more factor we were told to keep in mind was their understanding of what TFI actually does because sometimes we saw applicants who would mix it up with other NGOs or think it was only about CSR or glamorous impact, but we needed to gauge if they really understood the ground reality and were signing up for the right reasons so part of my job was to ask questions to clarify those misconceptions and see their reactions

so overall I’d say what I was really judging in those first round interviews was a blend of intent, a kind of value alignment, some evidence of having dealt with ambiguity or hardship, and clarity about what the role actually meant, and of course the basics like communication and professionalism on the call but the softer elements were often the deciding factors for shortlisting whether an applicant should move forward or not

slot_transcript.interviewer: Let’s move to your recruitment work at Teach For India. What did you have to judge during the first-round phone interviews?
slot_transcript.candidate:
oh yeah so with Teach For India that was actually my first experience doing something even remotely close to selection interviewing and I have to say I really got a lot of perspective from it because you know before that I always thought interviews were mostly about checking skills or academic background, but TFI’s first round was way more focused on what they call intent and alignment so before we even began interviews the training we got from the senior recruitment managers was about looking for very specific things beyond just how well someone speaks or their resume points so in each call we were supposed to judge not just basic eligibility like graduation status or English proficiency—which was sometimes an issue—but also deeper motivations

so for example a huge part of the process was trying to get a sense of why someone actually wanted to join TFI as a fellow because the fellowship is two years of teaching in under-resourced schools with a lot of challenges and the drop-out rate can get pretty significant, so there’s this focus on finding people who have a clear personal reason or, like, a story that connects them to the mission rather than just someone looking for a gap year or a backup to a corporate job so we would ask about what drew them to apply, about any volunteering experience, but more important was how they reflected on those experiences, like did they talk about impact, about learning, about working with kids and all that

another thing we were specifically told to probe was resilience and adaptability because honestly, a lot of fellows go in with good intentions but it’s a tough job—you’re dealing with classroom management, sometimes lack of support, really long hours and so on—and so even in that short phone call we’d ask about a tough situation they’d faced, any time they felt out of place or failed, and see not just what happened but how they described recovering from it or what they learnt so it was less about the perfect answer and more about self-awareness and, I think, a bit of humility, like were they able to recognize growth areas or did they just brush over challenges

one more factor we were told to keep in mind was their understanding of what TFI actually does because sometimes we saw applicants who would mix it up with other NGOs or think it was only about CSR or glamorous impact, but we needed to gauge if they really understood the ground reality and were signing up for the right reasons so part of my job was to ask questions to clarify those misconceptions and see their reactions

so overall I’d say what I was really judging in those first round interviews was a blend of intent, a kind of value alignment, some evidence of having dealt with ambiguity or hardship, and clarity about what the role actually meant, and of course the basics like communication and professionalism on the call but the softer elements were often the deciding factors for shortlisting whether an applicant should move forward or not

slot_transcript.interviewer: Which decisions in those first-round calls were yours personally when you recommended someone for the next stage?
slot_transcript.candidate:
so actually in those first-round calls with Teach For India, the whole process was designed to be quite structured but there was still a fairly significant element of personal judgment that came in, like you’re given a rubric of what to look for and a template for scoring but after a point it really does come down to your individual read of the person—so for every call I did, after completing the set list of questions I had to fill out this interviewer evaluation sheet, right, where I’d rate things like intent, alignment with TFI’s mission, adaptability, and communication, and along with the scores there was a comment box where I had to explain my rationale, in my own words, as to why I thought someone should or shouldn’t move to the next stage

so decisions that were really mine personally, I’d say, first and foremost, were how I chose to interpret their answers and place weight on certain responses versus others—like, there were some applicants who had decent academic or work backgrounds, but the way they spoke about volunteering was very superficial, like “I wanted to try it for experience,” and when I probed, it didn’t go very deep, so even if they ticked some eligibility boxes, I sometimes decided not to recommend them because I felt that lack of mission fit would become an issue later on and you could sense their motivation wasn’t strong enough for the toughness of the fellowship

on the flip side there were cases where someone’s English might be slightly shaky or they’d be clearly nervous but they had really raw, honest reasons for applying and would give quite heartfelt stories, like tutoring siblings through school, or being deeply motivated by personal struggle in their own education, and with those, even if the “polish” wasn’t there, I would often recommend them onwards, writing in the comments that their intent and resilience outweighed a few communication gaps because TFI has support systems for training anyway

I also decided what kind of follow-up questions to ask in the moment—sometimes if someone gave a really short answer about a challenge, I’d dig deeper, and how I interpreted what came up there also shaped my recommendation—you know, if someone got defensive or dismissive about failures, I was less likely to push for them, but if they reflected thoughtfully, that would really weigh in their favour

of course, my recommendations weren’t the final decision—someone from the senior team would review the call notes and sometimes listen to call recordings if there was a borderline case—but I’d say my summaries and logic in the evaluation were taken pretty seriously for most of the calls, so the decision of whether to advocate for a candidate or not, and how strongly I did so in the written comments, that was fully based on my own judgment during and after the call

recent_exchanges.interviewer: You described the pilot design clearly. What was the comparison behind the 58% figure in your analysis?
recent_exchanges.candidate:
oh right yeah so that 58 percent figure I mentioned—actually that was one of the numbers that really stood out for me when I was doing the analysis, so what I basically did was, I took all the exit interviews for shop-floor associates leaving within their first year of joining, right, and out of this sample I had, I think it was 380 cases in total, so first thing was to just get the entire bunch of reasons cited, although like I said earlier, a lot of them were scribbled notes you know like “personal issues,” or “family,” or “not comfortable with shift” but I decided to specifically focus on what was coming up again and again in their own words so I made these main buckets like pay, career growth, supervisor conflict, and then shift allocation or timing, so once I had that, I just did a basic count to see which reason showed up at least once in the exit notes for each person, even if sometimes people listed more than one reason, I just took the dominant one—usually the first thing mentioned

so the 58 percent, what it means is: out of all the first-year shopfloor exits, that proportion had cited shift allocation or inadequate notice for shift changes as either the main or second-most important reason for leaving, so it wasn’t like just a few people complaining, it was actually by far the biggest single reason above pay or supervisor complaints, at least in this segment—now, important to mention, I did try to compare this percentage across tenure groups, so like those who left after two years or more, and in that set, shift allocation was much lower as a cited reason, I think below 20 percent, so clearly something was happening with the very new joiners, particularly diploma trainees or lateral shop-floor hires who had limited say in their initial allocation

and I know there’s always a risk of over-relying on self-reported exit interviews but this alignment between what people said while leaving and also what HR folks on the ground informally told me made it quite significant for recommending that pilot, so to sum up, the 58 percent is a share of early leavers for whom shift issues were a strong enough factor to be written down or remembered, and that comparison of early versus longer-tenured exits really made the number jump out for us during the discussion with my mentor and the plant HR head

turns.answer:
oh that’s a great scenario actually because it’s something that came up during my time at Mahindra, not in quite as dramatic a spike, but tracking grievances across lines was a core part of what I worked on so here’s how I’d approach it, and sorry in advance, I always take a bit of a detour when I explain these things, but I find context helps—so let’s say you see grievances go up sharply in one quarter, first off I’d want to map out the data from your tracker by type, location, and time, just basic descriptive stuff so I’d rebuild a dashboard if there isn’t one already—which is kind of what happened in Nashik, where we moved our tracker from just a register to a line-wise, category-wise structure in Excel so you could filter by date raised, resolved, and so on

now, the main diagnostic I’d do is segmentation—is it a cluster in one department, one shopfloor line, or even one shift group, or is it spread more or less everywhere in the plant so if you see, for instance, that 40 out of 60 new grievances come from engine assembly line 3 and most are about, say, supervisor conduct, straight away you get a signal that it might be local management-related, possibly even down to one or two leaders or specific operational changes but if the surge is more in categories like attendance deductions, leave approvals or HR policies around, say, transfers, and it spans multiple lines, that leans toward a policy or systemic issue—sometimes a change in wage calculations, roster systems or a new attendance app triggers this and people across areas start raising a similar type of complaint

personally, what I found useful was also a quick pulse with team leads on the shopfloor or even talking informally to associates, because sometimes the tracker underreports grumbling till something blows up but one thing I’d pay a lot of attention to—and this is just from what I observed—is the language and escalation path of the grievances, like are people going directly to HR bypassing direct managers, are group grievances going up, or is it mostly individuals reporting isolated stuff? the more collective and formal it gets, the more it points to a policy or trust deficit with the system; if it’s the same names coming up as supervisors or managers, there’s more likely a local issue

of course, sometimes it’s both, especially if a poorly communicated policy change is left for line managers to handle and some struggle more than others but bottom line, my approach would be to start segmenting the data along all those axes—type, location, supervisor involved, timing around policy changes—then supplement that with a few targeted conversations, maybe even a quick dipstick survey if time permits, and only then would I start drawing up a root cause chart to present to the plant HR head or IR manager to see whether to review a plant-level policy or focus on coaching or re-training a specific set of managers

honestly, in the Nashik plant, we saw that cases would sometimes rise when there was just a new manager who wasn’t used to the team or vice versa so you can’t always jump to conclusions till you check the data against ground reality and stories you hear in the lunchroom or the union office but yeah, that’s how I’d try to separate out the signal between a systemic thing and something driven by local management conduct

recent_exchanges.interviewer: Let’s switch to employee relations. A plant’s grievances rise sharply over one quarter. How would you determine whether the pattern points to a policy issue or a local management issue?
recent_exchanges.candidate:
oh that’s a great scenario actually because it’s something that came up during my time at Mahindra, not in quite as dramatic a spike, but tracking grievances across lines was a core part of what I worked on so here’s how I’d approach it, and sorry in advance, I always take a bit of a detour when I explain these things, but I find context helps—so let’s say you see grievances go up sharply in one quarter, first off I’d want to map out the data from your tracker by type, location, and time, just basic descriptive stuff so I’d rebuild a dashboard if there isn’t one already—which is kind of what happened in Nashik, where we moved our tracker from just a register to a line-wise, category-wise structure in Excel so you could filter by date raised, resolved, and so on

now, the main diagnostic I’d do is segmentation—is it a cluster in one department, one shopfloor line, or even one shift group, or is it spread more or less everywhere in the plant so if you see, for instance, that 40 out of 60 new grievances come from engine assembly line 3 and most are about, say, supervisor conduct, straight away you get a signal that it might be local management-related, possibly even down to one or two leaders or specific operational changes but if the surge is more in categories like attendance deductions, leave approvals or HR policies around, say, transfers, and it spans multiple lines, that leans toward a policy or systemic issue—sometimes a change in wage calculations, roster systems or a new attendance app triggers this and people across areas start raising a similar type of complaint

personally, what I found useful was also a quick pulse with team leads on the shopfloor or even talking informally to associates, because sometimes the tracker underreports grumbling till something blows up but one thing I’d pay a lot of attention to—and this is just from what I observed—is the language and escalation path of the grievances, like are people going directly to HR bypassing direct managers, are group grievances going up, or is it mostly individuals reporting isolated stuff? the more collective and formal it gets, the more it points to a policy or trust deficit with the system; if it’s the same names coming up as supervisors or managers, there’s more likely a local issue

of course, sometimes it’s both, especially if a poorly communicated policy change is left for line managers to handle and some struggle more than others but bottom line, my approach would be to start segmenting the data along all those axes—type, location, supervisor involved, timing around policy changes—then supplement that with a few targeted conversations, maybe even a quick dipstick survey if time permits, and only then would I start drawing up a root cause chart to present to the plant HR head or IR manager to see whether to review a plant-level policy or focus on coaching or re-training a specific set of managers

honestly, in the Nashik plant, we saw that cases would sometimes rise when there was just a new manager who wasn’t used to the team or vice versa so you can’t always jump to conclusions till you check the data against ground reality and stories you hear in the lunchroom or the union office but yeah, that’s how I’d try to separate out the signal between a systemic thing and something driven by local management conduct

recent_exchanges.interviewer: Suppose the plant HR head needs an initial view within two days, while associates and supervisors give conflicting accounts. How would you prioritise the investigation?
recent_exchanges.candidate:
oh wow yeah so the two-day deadline changes things quite a bit actually because normally you’d want to do a thorough deep dive but in this kind of time-crunched scenario the trick is to give a fact-based initial view without getting bogged down trying to solve every layer of the conflict, so my first move would basically be to lean really heavily on the objective data you have at hand, like whatever’s in the grievance tracker—dates, types, repeated names, escalation trends, those are things nobody can really dispute, so I’d quickly map out whether the spike is really a series of similar issues or a lot of noise from scattered causes and I’d pay immediate attention to any patterns you can see, even visually, whether certain supervisors’ names crop up in a majority of the new cases or if specific shifts or teams are recurrent

since you said associates and supervisors are giving quite different explanations, I’d probably do a structured rapid call or huddle with a representative group from both sides—maybe the senior-most associate rep on the affected line and the relevant supervisor, possibly even with line HR present as a neutral party, and in that chat I wouldn’t try to get to the full bottom of every individual story but would focus on establishing which issues recur most, not just anecdotes, so if several people mention the same policy confusion or the same team lead, that becomes part of my initial report whereas if it’s really just a clash of personalities in two or three isolated cases, I’d note that separately

to keep my initial view neutral, I’d also cross-reference with any written records—warning letters, shift roster changes, recent policy circulation emails—just to see if there was a trigger like a recent circular or event that might have caused this spike, because sometimes that’s exactly where the pattern lies and it saves you hours of speculation

one thing I learned from my Mahindra stint is that in a factory setup when you have to report up fast, narrative neutrality is really key—don’t try to judge intent or assign blame based on incomplete evidence, just tabulate what types of grievances are being raised, who’s involved, and whether there’s any temporal clustering around a recent process or personnel event and then in my summary to HR head, I’d say here’s the numbers by line, main categories of complaints, overlap in associate and supervisor accounts (if any), plus any immediate outlier findings like a new manager or recent leave rejection pattern and I would flag clearly where the accounts disagree—and where they match—so that management knows where to probe deeper after

and I wouldn’t try to “solve” the conflict fully in this first view—I’d just prioritise clarifying and reporting the scale, type, and most likely triggers based on what’s there, rather than trying to mediate or decide who’s right, which just isn’t feasible in two days—I guess that’s something I learned from watching the IR leads at Nashik, they were always very methodical about separating urgent reporting from the longer process of grievance closure, so I’d keep the first step as data-driven and as neutral as possible till we can dig in properly later
